q-and-le-chatelier-s1.title: Q right after three changes
q-and-le-chatelier-s1.text: For N2O4(g) ⇌ 2 NO2(g) at a fixed temperature, Kc = 4.6 × 10−3. A flask at equilibrium is changed in three separate experiments, each at constant temperature. The table gives the concentrations immediately after each change, before any reaction.

table.caption: Concentrations and Q immediately after each change

q-and-le-chatelier-s2.title: Adding X₂ to an equilibrium mixture
q-and-le-chatelier-s2.html:
Key: X2Y2XY

For X2(g) + Y2(g) ⇌ 2 XY(g), the left container is at equilibrium. Three X2 molecules are then injected at constant temperature and volume.

items.q: Which statement correctly justifies the shift after change A?
options: Q > K, so the net reaction goes in reverse.
K increases because NO<sub>2</sub> was added, so the system shifts forward.
The reverse reaction speeds up, so the system shifts toward NO<sub>2</sub>.
Q < K, so the net reaction goes forward.

why.correct: After a concentration change, compare the new Q with the unchanged K. Q > K: net reverse.
options: Right: adding NO₂ raised Q to 2.3 × 10⁻² while K stayed 4.6 × 10⁻³.
K does not change with concentration. The added NO₂ changes Q.
A faster reverse reaction makes N₂O₄, not NO₂. And a justification should compare Q with K.
Q = 2.3 × 10⁻² is larger than K = 4.6 × 10⁻³, not smaller.

items.q: After change B (volume doubled), which way does the system shift and why?
options: Forward: halving each concentration halves Q.
No shift, because both concentrations were halved equally.
In reverse, because a larger volume favors fewer gas moles.
Forward, because doubling the volume doubles K.

why.correct: Volume changes alter every concentration, and Q changes whenever the gas coefficients differ. Q < K means net forward, toward more gas molecules, consistent with Le Châtelier.
options: Right: Q = [NO₂]²/[N₂O₄] has two factors on top and one on the bottom; halving all of them halves Q, to 2.3 × 10<sup>−3</sup>.
Equal halving cancels only when the exponents on top and bottom match. Here they are 2 and 1.
A larger volume favors more gas moles. The products side has 2 mol gas versus 1.
Volume does not change K; it changes Q.

items.q: After change C, what happens to [NO<sub>2</sub>] as the system returns to equilibrium?
options: It decreases, because Q > K and the net reaction runs in reverse.
It increases, because Q > K and the net reaction runs forward.
It stays the same, because NO<sub>2</sub> was not changed.
It increases, because the removed N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> is replaced by NO<sub>2</sub>.

why.correct: Q = (0.0136)² / 0.0200 = 9.2 × 10<sup>−3</sup> > K, so the net reaction goes in reverse: NO₂ is used to form N₂O₄.
options: Right: removing N₂O₄ lowered the denominator, so Q rose above K; the reverse reaction uses NO₂ to re-form N₂O₄.
Q > K means net reverse, which uses NO₂.
Q no longer equals K, so every concentration changes until it does.
Replacing N₂O₄ means making N₂O₄, which uses NO₂.

items.q: Calculate Q<sub>c</sub> right after change A.

mistakes.why: Value: [NO₂] must be squared, because its coefficient is 2.
Value: you inverted Q. Products go on top.

items.q: In a fourth experiment, the flask is heated. The reaction is endothermic. How should the shift be justified?
options: K rises, so now Q < K: net forward.
Q increases with temperature, so the mixture shifts in reverse.
K stays the same, but the forward rate increases, so it shifts forward.
Heat is a product, so the system shifts in reverse.

why.correct: For a temperature change, K itself changes. Endothermic: K rises on heating, so Q (unchanged) is now below K, and the net reaction goes forward.
options: Right: here K changes, not Q. With the old concentrations, Q is now less than the new, larger K.
Heating a sealed flask does not change the concentrations at once, so Q does not change. K does.
A temperature change does change K. A justification must say so.
For an endothermic reaction, heat is like a reactant, not a product.

items.q: Using particle counts (the gas moles are equal on both sides), calculate K for this reaction.

mistakes.why: Value: [XY] is squared, because its coefficient is 2.

items.q: Which justification of the shift after X<sub>2</sub> is added would earn full credit?
options: Q = 4²/(5 × 2) = 1.6 < K = 4.0, so net forward until Q = K.
Adding X<sub>2</sub> to the container increases K, so more XY forms.
The system wants to use up the extra X<sub>2</sub>, so it shifts right.
Adding X<sub>2</sub> speeds up the forward reaction, so it shifts right.

why.correct: A full-credit justification compares Q with K: here Q = 1.6 < K = 4.0, so the net reaction goes forward.
options: Right: claim (direction), evidence (the value of Q from the counts) and reasoning (comparison with the unchanged K).
K does not change with concentration. This answer would lose the point.
Systems do not "want" anything; a justification needs Q compared with K.
This is rate language alone. On the exam, a shift is justified with Q vs K.

items.q: Compared with the left container, how do the amounts in the right container compare once equilibrium is restored?
options: More X<sub>2</sub>, less Y<sub>2</sub>, more XY
The same amounts of each as in the left container
Less X<sub>2</sub>, more Y<sub>2</sub> and less XY than the left container
More X<sub>2</sub>, the same Y<sub>2</sub> and the same XY as the left container

why.correct: Q < K, so the net reaction goes forward: Y₂ falls, XY rises, and X₂ falls from 5 but stays above the original 2, because the shift only partly counteracts the change.
options: Right: the shift uses part of the added X₂ (so X₂ ends above 2), uses some Y₂ (below 2) and makes XY (above 4).
The added X atoms cannot vanish; the new equilibrium has a different composition with the same K.
This describes a reverse shift, but Q < K after adding X₂.
With Q < K there must be a net forward reaction, which changes Y₂ and XY as well.

items.q: Immediately after the X<sub>2</sub> is added, which rate has changed?
options: The forward rate has increased.
The reverse rate has increased.
Both rates have increased equally.
Neither rate has changed.

why.correct: The rate picture and the Q picture agree: Q < K is the same situation as forward rate > reverse rate.
options: Right: more X₂ means more X₂-Y₂ collisions each second. This matches Q < K.
The reverse reaction uses XY, which is unchanged at that instant.
Only the forward reaction uses X₂.
The forward rate depends on [X₂], which has risen.

items.q: CaCO<sub>3</sub>(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO<sub>2</sub>(g) is at equilibrium in a sealed container. Some CO<sub>2</sub> is pumped out at constant temperature. Which justification is correct?
options: Q = P<sub>CO₂</sub> drops below K<sub>p</sub>, so more CaCO<sub>3</sub> decomposes until P<sub>CO₂</sub> returns to K<sub>p</sub>.
K<sub>p</sub> drops, so the system shifts in reverse.
There is no shift, because the solids are unchanged.
Q rises above K<sub>p</sub>, so CO<sub>2</sub> is used up.

why.correct: Here Q = P<sub>CO₂</sub>. Pumping out CO₂ makes Q < K, so the net forward reaction makes CO₂ until P<sub>CO₂</sub> = K<sub>p</sub> again, the same pressure as before.
options: Right: with Q = P<sub>CO₂</sub>, removing gas makes Q < K and the net reaction goes forward.
Removing a gas changes Q, not K.
The solids are not in Q, but CO₂ is, and it changed.
Lowering P<sub>CO₂</sub> lowers Q.

items.q: For N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 3 H<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NH<sub>3</sub>(g) at equilibrium, the volume is suddenly halved at constant temperature. By what factor does Q change at that instant? (Give Q<sub>new</sub> / Q<sub>old</sub>.)

mistakes.why: Value: every concentration doubles. The top has (2)² and the bottom (2)(2)³ = 16, so Q changes by 4/16.
Value: you only counted the top. The bottom grows by 2 × 2³ = 16, so Q falls to 4/16 of its value.

why.correct: Each concentration doubles. Q<sub>new</sub> = (2[NH₃])² / ((2[N₂])(2[H₂])³) = 4/16 × Q<sub>old</sub> = 0.25 Q<sub>old</sub>. Q < K, so the net reaction goes forward, toward fewer gas moles.

items.q: For an exothermic reaction at equilibrium, the temperature is lowered. Which statement is correct?
options: K increases, so Q < K: shift to products.
K decreases; Q > K, so it shifts toward reactants.
K stays the same; Q decreases, so it shifts toward products.
Neither Q nor K changes, so there is no shift.

why.correct: Temperature changes K. For an exothermic forward reaction, K is larger at lower temperature, so Q (unchanged) < K and the net reaction goes forward.
options: Right: cooling favors the exothermic direction, which shows up as a larger K.
For an exothermic reaction, cooling increases K.
Cooling changes K, not Q (the concentrations do not change at that instant).
K depends on temperature, so it changes.

items.q: Which statements are valid justifications on a free-response question? Select all that apply.
options: "Adding H<sub>2</sub> makes Q < K, so the net reaction proceeds forward until Q = K."
"Raising the temperature increases K for this endothermic reaction, so Q < K and the reaction shifts forward."
"Adding H<sub>2</sub> increases K, so more product forms."
"The reaction shifts right to relieve the stress."

why.correct: A justification names what changed (Q, or K for a temperature change) and compares Q with K to give the direction.
options: Right: names the change in Q and compares it with K.
Right: identifies that K changes with temperature and uses the comparison.
K does not change with concentration.
This restates Le Châtelier without evidence or reasoning; readers do not award it.

items.q: For 2 SO<sub>2</sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 SO<sub>3</sub>(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 280. A mixture has Q = 280. Then SO<sub>2</sub> and SO<sub>3</sub> are both doubled in concentration at constant temperature, with O<sub>2</sub> unchanged. What happens?
options: No shift, since Q is still 280.
Forward shift: more reactant was added.
Reverse shift: more product was added.
K doubles, so the system shifts forward.

why.correct: Calculate the new Q rather than guessing. The factors of 4 on top and bottom cancel, so Q still equals K and there is no shift.
options: Product was added in the same proportion; Q is unchanged.
Reactant was added in the same proportion; Q is unchanged.
K does not change with concentration.

items.q: Put the parts of a full-credit justification for an equilibrium shift in order.
options: State what the change does to Q (or to K, if the temperature changed).
Compare the new Q with K, giving the inequality.
State the direction of the net reaction that follows from the comparison.
State that the reaction continues until Q = K again.

why.correct: Claim, evidence and reasoning: what changed, the comparison, the direction, and when it stops.
